findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the command shell
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax such as `main; arbitrary-command` or `$(arbitrary-command)`, `exec()` executes it with the application's privileges instead of passing it literally to Git. Restore argument-based process invocation such as `execFile("git", ["show", branch])`.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve the branch name as a single process argument
findings.body:
On POSIX shells, a valid Git branch such as `HEAD;sleep${IFS}30;true` is interpreted as three ordered commands. `showBranch` therefore shows `HEAD`, waits 30 seconds, and reports success from `true` instead of showing the requested branch. This corrupts the child process’s completion timing and exit status.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the command shell
findings.body:
`exec()` interpolates `branch` into a shell command. On Unix, an input such as `main; arbitrary-command` executes the appended command with the application’s privileges; shell substitutions such as `$(...)` also execute. The previous `execFile()` implementation passed the value as a literal argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restore `execFile` argument passing to prevent shell command injection
findings.body:
`exec()` runs through a shell, so any caller-controlled branch value containing syntax such as `main; arbitrary-command` or `$(arbitrary-command)` executes commands with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` treated the entire value as a Git argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
